title: Review: Lighting Controls and Emergency Lighting

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: School corridor after hours, exit sign and emergency battery unit visible. Matthew mid-corridor. Medium shot.
scenes.on_screen: Review: Lighting Controls and Emergency Lighting
scenes.says: This review covers controls from LT3 and LT4, and emergency lighting from LT3. Controls save energy. Emergency lighting saves lives. Any test that interrupts power gets coordinated so occupied egress paths are never left dark. Let's walk through each device.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Classroom: Matthew points to a ceiling-mounted dual-technology occupancy sensor.
scenes.on_screen:
PIR: line of sight - Ultrasonic: around obstacles, airflow false trips - Dual-tech: both to turn on, either to hold - Microwave: sees through walls
Occupancy = auto-on - Vacancy = manual-on
scenes.says: Sensors. PIR sees heat movement but needs line of sight and misses small motions far away. Ultrasonic sees around obstacles but can false-trigger from airflow. Dual-technology typically needs both to turn on and either to hold on, so fewer false trips. Microwave is very sensitive and can see through walls. Occupancy is auto-on, auto-off. Vacancy is manual-on, auto-off.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Electrical room, panel closed: Matthew points to a lighting contactor enclosure and a time clock; cut to a rooftop photocell.
scenes.on_screen:
Photocell: aim north, away from controlled lights
Mechanically held: stays put - Electrically held: drops out on coil power loss
scenes.says: Exterior controls. Photocells turn lights on at dusk; aim them north where possible and away from the lights they control. Astronomical time clocks calculate sunrise and sunset by location. Contactors switch big lighting loads from a small control circuit. Mechanically held ones stay in position without coil power. Electrically held ones drop out when coil power is lost.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Classroom: networked room controller on the wall; laptop showing a fixture group map.
scenes.on_screen:
NLC - LLLC - high-end trim - BACnet
Energy codes: manual control, auto shutoff, multi-level, daylight, exterior, testing, LPD
scenes.says: Networked controls can be wired, wireless mesh, or hybrid. Luminaire-level control gives each fixture its own sensor. High-end trim, or task tuning, cuts maximum output to what's needed. BMS integration is often BACnet. Energy codes require local manual control, automatic shutoff, multi-level control, daylight controls, exterior controls and functional testing, and they limit lighting power density. Check the adopted edition.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Corridor: Matthew points to the exit sign, the emergency battery unit, then a UL 924 transfer device near a controlled fixture.
scenes.on_screen: NFPA 101: when, where, performance - NEC 700: emergency wiring - UL 924: equipment
scenes.says: Emergency lighting. NFPA 101, the Life Safety Code, says when and where it's required and how it performs. NEC Article 700 covers emergency system wiring. UL 924 covers the equipment: exit signs, battery units, and control devices that force switched or dimmed fixtures to emergency output when normal power is lost.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.on_screen:
1.5 hours - average 1 fc - minimum 0.1 fc - max-to-min 40:1
End of 1.5 h: 0.6 fc avg, 0.06 fc min
scenes.says: The numbers. At least 1.5 hours after power loss. Initially, an average of at least 1 foot-candle and a minimum of 0.1 at any point along the egress path, measured at the floor, with max-to-min no more than 40 to 1. By the end of the 1.5 hours, it can drop to 0.6 average and 0.06 minimum.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Senior tech presses the test button on an emergency battery unit, times 30 seconds with a stopwatch, then writes a test log entry.
scenes.on_screen: Monthly: at least 30 seconds - Annually: 90 minutes - Keep written records
scenes.says: Testing battery equipment. Monthly, at intervals not over 30 days, a functional test of at least 30 seconds. Annually, the full 90 minutes. Keep written records for the AHJ. Self-testing units can automate it, but records and follow-up on failures are still required. A unit fails its 30 seconds? Think dead battery, failed charger, failed lamp, or not on an unswitched circuit.

scenes.speaker: Matthew Berrett
scenes.background: Matthew in the corridor, medium close-up. Safety callout.
scenes.on_screen:
Disconnect the battery per the manufacturer before working on an emergency unit's wiring.
Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: Remember, an emergency unit may be on an unswitched circuit and it has a battery. Disconnect the battery per the manufacturer before working on its wiring, and don't modify emergency circuits or transfer equipment without authorization and LOTO. Controlled fixtures staying off in an outage? Check the UL 924 device. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Electrical room panel stays closed throughout. Emergency unit test in scene 7 is the unit's own test button only; no circuits opened. Test log shown is a generic form. School setting must be generic with no school names or logos; film after hours.
